To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a personalized brain model for each of 15 patients with partial drug-resistant epilepsy.
personalized virtual brain models derived with the use of diffusion magnetic resonance imaging can predict seizure propagation and explain the variability in surgery outcomes.
we have shown that personalized virtual brain models derived using diffusion imaging can be used to improve the diagnosis and treatment of drug-resistant epilepsy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of personalized virtual brain models for the understanding of brain disorders.
the development of a personalized virtual brain platform for the exploration and prediction of brain function and dysfunction.
the development and evaluation of personalized brain network models to improve diagnosis and treatment of epilepsy and other neurological and psychiatric diseases.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the brain network model has the capacity to account for the observed seizure propagation patterns, but does not reliably augment with use of the patient-specific connectivity.

the use of personalized connectome-based brain models is an important step forward in understanding the mechanisms underlying brain function and disease and that it is a valuable tool for personalized medicine in the future.
connectome-based models have the capacity for personalized in silico testing of clinical hypotheses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown how to create a patient-specific virtual brain that can explain the patient's seizure pattern and can predict seizure propagation in the patient's brain.
we can use the patient's own brain to understand the brain.
the individual brain structure and the modelling predict seizure propagation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
connectome-based models can be used as a personalized in silico brain to test and validate clinical hypotheses, thus providing an alternative to the traditional in vivo animal and human studies.
patient-specific virtual human brain models are now feasible and can provide new insights into the mechanisms of brain disorders and their treatment.

the combination of non-invasive neuroimaging and mathematical modelling can lead to the development of a personalized in silico platform that has the capacity to explain clinical phenomena and to generate testable hypotheses for clinical trials.
